name: Jeffrey Lionel Dahmer
victimProfile: Young men and boys, predominantly African American, aged 14 to 33, often from marginalized communities
captureMethod: Intended victim Tracy Edwards escaped Dahmer's apartment in handcuffs and flagged down Milwaukee police officers, who returned to the apartment and discovered photographs of dismembered bodies.
sentence: 16 consecutive life terms totaling 941 years in prison without possibility of parole
fateDetail: Beaten to death by fellow inmate Christopher Scarver at Columbia Correctional Institution in Portage, Wisconsin on November 28, 1994
summary: Jeffrey Dahmer murdered 17 men and boys in Wisconsin and Ohio between 1978 and 1991. Known as the Milwaukee Cannibal, his crimes involved drugging, dismemberment, necrophilia, and cannibalism.
narrative: Jeffrey Lionel Dahmer, born May 21, 1960, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, became one of the most notorious serial killers in American history. Raised in Bath Township, Ohio, a middle-class suburb of Akron, Dahmer exhibited troubling behavior from a young age, including a fascination with dead animals and their bones. His parents' turbulent marriage ended in divorce in 1978, leaving the eighteen-year-old largely unsupervised in the family home. According to Biography.com and multiple court records, this isolation coincided with the beginning of his criminal career.

Dahmer committed his first murder on June 18, 1978, shortly after graduating from Revere High School in Ohio. He picked up eighteen-year-old hitchhiker Steven Hicks, brought him back to his parents' home, and killed him after Hicks tried to leave. Dahmer dismembered the body, dissolved the flesh in acid, and crushed the bones with a sledgehammer, scattering the remains in the woods behind the house. Following this killing, Dahmer briefly attended Ohio State University before enlisting in the United States Army in 1979. He was stationed in Germany but was discharged in 1981 due to alcohol problems, as documented by Murderpedia and the Crime Museum.

After his discharge, Dahmer moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where he lived with his grandmother before eventually securing his own apartment at 924 North 25th Street. According to court testimony reported by the Associated Press, Dahmer's killing resumed in September 1987 when he murdered Steven Tuomi at the Ambassador Hotel. Over the next four years, the frequency of his crimes accelerated dramatically. He killed two men in 1988, one in 1989, four in 1990, and eight in 1991 alone. His method became increasingly ritualistic: he would lure young men to his apartment with offers of money or alcohol, drug them with sleeping pills, and strangle them.

What set Dahmer apart from other serial killers was the post-mortem nature of his crimes. According to testimony presented during his trial, covered extensively by the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, Dahmer engaged in necrophilia, dismemberment, and cannibalism. He preserved body parts as trophies, including skulls that he painted and kept on a shelf. He experimented with creating so-called zombies by drilling into his victims' skulls and injecting muriatic acid into their brains while they were still alive, in an effort to render them permanently compliant. Police discovered photographs documenting these acts upon his arrest.

One of the most disturbing episodes occurred on May 27, 1991, when fourteen-year-old Konerak Sinthasomphone was found wandering the streets naked and disoriented. Two women called police, but when officers arrived, Dahmer convinced them the boy was his adult lover who had simply had too much to drink. The officers returned Sinthasomphone to Dahmer's apartment without verifying his age or identity. Dahmer killed the boy shortly after the police left. This incident, reported by the New York Times and confirmed in subsequent investigations, led to the firing of the officers involved and widespread criticism of the Milwaukee Police Department.

Dahmer's reign of terror ended on July 22, 1991, when Tracy Edwards, whom Dahmer had lured to his apartment, managed to escape while still handcuffed. Edwards flagged down a patrol car and led Officers Rolf Mueller and Robert Rauth back to Dahmer's apartment. Inside, the officers discovered Polaroid photographs of dismembered bodies, a barrel containing acid and decomposing remains, and severed heads stored in the refrigerator. Dahmer was arrested immediately. According to the Wisconsin Court of Appeals records, he subsequently confessed to seventeen murders spanning thirteen years.

Dahmer's trial began on January 30, 1992, in Milwaukee County Circuit Court before Judge Laurence Gram. Having already pleaded guilty to fifteen counts of murder in Wisconsin, the sole issue before the jury was his sanity at the time of the crimes. On February 15, 1992, the jury found Dahmer sane and guilty, and Judge Gram sentenced him to sixteen consecutive life terms, totaling 941 years in prison. He received an additional life sentence in Ohio for the murder of Steven Hicks. Dahmer was incarcerated at the Columbia Correctional Institution in Portage, Wisconsin.

On November 28, 1994, Dahmer was beaten to death by fellow inmate Christopher Scarver while on a work detail in the prison gymnasium. Scarver also killed another inmate, Jesse Anderson, during the same incident. Dahmer was pronounced dead at a local hospital approximately one hour after the attack. His case remains a landmark in criminal psychology and forensic investigation, prompting significant reforms in law enforcement procedures and sex offender registries across the United States.

name: John Wayne Gacy Jr.
victimProfile: Teenage boys and young men, predominantly aged 14 to 21, many of whom were employees or acquaintances recruited through Gacy's construction business
captureMethod: The disappearance of 15-year-old Robert Piest led investigators to Gacy. A search warrant revealed human remains buried in the crawl space beneath his home.
sentence: Death sentence; 12 death sentences and 21 natural life sentences
fateDetail: Executed by lethal injection at Stateville Correctional Center in Crest Hill, Illinois on May 10, 1994
summary: John Wayne Gacy, the Killer Clown, murdered 33 young men and boys in suburban Chicago between 1972 and 1978, burying most of the remains in the crawl space beneath his home.
narrative: John Wayne Gacy Jr. was born on March 17, 1942, in Chicago, Illinois, the second of three children. He grew up in a working-class neighborhood on the city's North Side, where his father was a machinist and World War I veteran who struggled with alcoholism and frequently abused the family. According to Britannica and court testimony records, Gacy was a largely unremarkable student who suffered from a congenital heart condition that prevented him from participating in sports, a fact that drew further ridicule from his father.

Gacy moved to Waterloo, Iowa, in the mid-1960s, where he managed a Kentucky Fried Chicken franchise owned by his father-in-law. It was during this period that his criminal behavior first came to light. In 1968, he was indicted on charges of sodomy involving a teenage boy, and subsequently convicted. He was sentenced to ten years in the Iowa State Men's Reformatory but was paroled after serving just eighteen months, according to court records documented by AETV. His wife divorced him during his incarceration, and he lost all contact with his two children.

After his release in 1970, Gacy returned to the Chicago area and settled in Norwood Park Township, an unincorporated community in Cook County. He started a construction company, PDM Contractors, and became active in local Democratic politics and community organizations. He was known for performing as Pogo the Clown at children's parties and charitable events, a persona that would later earn him the nickname 'Killer Clown' in the national press. According to Biography.com, Gacy projected the image of a successful, community-minded businessman, which helped him evade suspicion for years.

Gacy's first known murder occurred in January 1972, when he killed sixteen-year-old Timothy McCoy. As documented in trial records and confirmed by the Cook County State's Attorney, Gacy had picked up McCoy at a Greyhound bus station and brought him to his home, where he stabbed the teenager to death. Over the following six years, Gacy murdered at least thirty-two more young men and boys, with the heaviest concentration of killings occurring between 1976 and 1978. His method typically involved luring victims to his home under the pretense of offering construction work, then restraining them with handcuffs or a rope trick he demonstrated as a game, before strangling or asphyxiating them.

Gacy buried twenty-six of his victims in the crawl space beneath his house, placed three others elsewhere on his property, and disposed of his last four known victims by throwing their bodies into the Des Plaines River. According to History.com and the Cook County Medical Examiner's office, the remains were in various states of decomposition, and eight victims were so badly deteriorated that they could not be identified for decades. Advanced DNA technology and forensic genealogy have since led to the identification of several previously unknown victims, though at least one remains unidentified as of 2024.

The investigation that brought Gacy down began on December 11, 1978, when fifteen-year-old Robert Piest disappeared after telling his mother he was going to talk to a contractor about a job. Witnesses placed Piest with Gacy, and investigators quickly discovered Gacy's 1968 sodomy conviction in Iowa. A search warrant was obtained, and on December 21, 1978, police began excavating the crawl space under Gacy's home. Gacy confessed to police the following day, detailing dozens of murders. He was formally arrested and charged with multiple counts of murder.

Gacy's trial began on February 6, 1980, in the Cook County Criminal Courts Building. His defense attorneys argued that he was insane at the time of the murders, presenting testimony from psychiatric experts. The prosecution countered with evidence that Gacy had carefully concealed his crimes and continued to function normally in society. According to trial transcripts referenced by Britannica, the jury deliberated for less than two hours before returning guilty verdicts on all thirty-three murder charges on March 13, 1980. Gacy was sentenced to death for twelve of the murders and received twenty-one natural life sentences for the remainder.

During his fourteen years on death row at the Menard Correctional Center, Gacy painted numerous oil paintings, many depicting clowns, which were sold to collectors and attracted significant controversy. He exhausted all his appeals by 1994. On May 10, 1994, John Wayne Gacy was executed by lethal injection at the Stateville Correctional Center in Crest Hill, Illinois. His final words were reportedly a defiant insult directed at his executioners. The case prompted lasting reforms in missing-persons investigations and coordination between jurisdictions, and it remains one of the most prolific serial murder cases in American criminal history.

name: Theodore Robert Bundy
victimProfile: Young women and girls, predominantly white, college-aged, often with long dark hair parted in the middle
captureMethod: Arrested during a routine traffic stop in Pensacola, Florida after a patrol officer noticed Bundy driving a stolen Volkswagen Beetle. He had previously escaped custody twice in Colorado.
sentence: Three death sentences for the murders of Lisa Levy, Margaret Bowman, and Kimberly Leach in Florida
fateDetail: Executed in the electric chair at Florida State Prison in Starke, Florida on January 24, 1989
summary: Ted Bundy confessed to 30 murders across seven states during the 1970s. A charismatic law student, he escaped custody twice before his final arrest in Florida, where he was executed in 1989.
narrative: Theodore Robert Bundy was born on November 24, 1946, in Burlington, Vermont, to Eleanor Louise Cowell, an unmarried mother. His biological father's identity was never conclusively established. Bundy was initially raised by his maternal grandparents and was led to believe his mother was his sister, a deception he did not uncover until adulthood. According to Britannica and multiple biographical accounts, the family relocated to Tacoma, Washington, in 1950, where his mother married Johnnie Bundy, whose surname Ted adopted. He grew up outwardly normal, performing well academically and becoming involved in politics as a young man.

Bundy attended the University of Puget Sound and later transferred to the University of Washington, where he studied psychology. According to Biography.com, he worked at a crisis hotline and became involved with the Republican Party, projecting an image of ambition and charm. He was accepted to law school at the University of Utah in 1974 and relocated to Salt Lake City. Investigators would later determine that this period coincided with the beginning of a multi-state murder spree that would claim at least thirty lives across seven states.

The earliest confirmed murders attributed to Bundy occurred in Washington State in early 1974. According to the ABC News timeline and court records, young women began disappearing from college campuses in the Pacific Northwest, including Lynda Ann Healy from the University of Washington on January 31, 1974, and Susan Rancourt from Central Washington State University on April 17, 1974. Witnesses at Lake Sammamish State Park on July 14, 1974, reported a man calling himself Ted who wore a fake arm cast and asked women for help loading a sailboat onto his car. Two women, Janice Ott and Denise Naslund, disappeared that day.

After relocating to Utah, Bundy continued killing. He was first arrested on August 16, 1975, when a Utah Highway Patrol officer stopped him for suspicious driving and discovered handcuffs, a ski mask, and an ice pick in his vehicle. He was subsequently identified by surviving victim Carol DaRonch and convicted of aggravated kidnapping in 1976, receiving a one-to-fifteen-year sentence. While awaiting trial for the murder of Caryn Campbell in Colorado, Bundy escaped from the Pitkin County Courthouse in Aspen on June 7, 1977, by jumping from a second-floor window. He was recaptured eight days later.

Bundy's second escape proved far more consequential. On December 30, 1977, he crawled through a ceiling hole in his cell at the Garfield County Jail in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, and fled to Florida. According to court records from the State of Florida and reporting by the Tallahassee Democrat, Bundy attacked four women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University on January 15, 1978, killing Margaret Bowman and Lisa Levy and severely injuring two others. Three weeks later, on February 9, 1978, he abducted and murdered twelve-year-old Kimberly Leach from her junior high school in Lake City, Florida.

Bundy was arrested for the final time on February 15, 1978, during a traffic stop in Pensacola, Florida, while driving a stolen Volkswagen Beetle. He was tried and convicted in two separate Florida trials. In July 1979, a jury in Miami convicted him of the Chi Omega murders and sentenced him to death by electrocution. A second trial in Orlando in February 1980 resulted in another death sentence for the murder of Kimberly Leach. According to the Florida Supreme Court records, Bundy used his legal training to participate in his own defense, at one point proposing to his girlfriend during testimony.

In the years following his conviction, Bundy granted numerous interviews to researchers and journalists while exhausting his appeals. In the final days before his execution, he confessed to approximately thirty murders in conversations with investigators from multiple states, though he provided varying levels of detail. According to reporting by HistoryLink.org and the Associated Press, many law enforcement officials believed his true victim count was considerably higher, with some estimates exceeding one hundred. DNA evidence has continued to link Bundy to additional cold cases, including the 2026 confirmation of his responsibility for the 1974 murder of Melissa Ann Smith in Utah.

Ted Bundy was executed in Florida's electric chair at Florida State Prison in Starke on January 24, 1989, at the age of forty-two. A crowd gathered outside the prison cheered when his death was announced. His case fundamentally changed how law enforcement agencies coordinate across state lines in serial murder investigations, and it remains one of the most studied cases in the history of criminal profiling.

Convicted in Miami for the Chi Omega murders; sentenced to death

name: Ricardo Leyva Munoz Ramirez
victimProfile: Victims varied widely in age, gender, and ethnicity; included individuals and couples in their homes, ranging from children to the elderly
captureMethod: After police publicly identified Ramirez through fingerprints found in a stolen car, residents of an East Los Angeles neighborhood recognized him from media photos and subdued him until police arrived.
sentence: Death sentence; 19 death sentences plus additional 59 years and four months in prison for 30 other felonies
fateDetail: Died of B-cell lymphoma on death row at San Quentin State Prison on June 7, 2013, at age 53
summary: Richard Ramirez, the Night Stalker, terrorized the Los Angeles and San Francisco areas in 1984-85 with a series of home-invasion murders, sexual assaults, and burglaries. Convicted of 13 murders.
narrative: Ricardo Leyva Munoz Ramirez was born on February 29, 1960, in El Paso, Texas, the youngest of five children in a Mexican-American family. His father, Julian Ramirez, was a laborer on the Santa Fe railroad. According to court records and reporting by Refinery29, Ramirez suffered head injuries as a child that reportedly caused epileptic seizures. At the age of thirteen, he fell under the influence of his older cousin Miguel, a decorated Green Beret who had returned from Vietnam and shared graphic stories and photographs of violence. In 1973, Ramirez witnessed Miguel fatally shoot his wife during a domestic argument, an event that multiple biographers cite as a formative trauma.

Ramirez drifted to California in the late 1970s, gravitating toward the criminal underworld of Los Angeles. He developed addictions to cocaine and PCP, sustained himself through petty theft and burglary, and became increasingly obsessed with Satanism. According to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's records and reporting by Biography.com, his criminal evolution from burglar to serial killer accelerated rapidly. The first murder attributed to the Night Stalker was that of seventy-nine-year-old Jennie Vincow, who was sexually assaulted and stabbed to death during a burglary of her Glassell Park home on June 28, 1984.

The majority of Ramirez's crimes occurred during a terrifying five-month period between March and August 1985. According to trial testimony reported by the UPI and the Los Angeles Times, he broke into homes across the greater Los Angeles area, typically late at night, using whatever weapons were available. His attacks were marked by extreme brutality and randomness: he shot, stabbed, bludgeoned, and strangled victims without apparent pattern. He sexually assaulted many of his surviving victims and forced them to swear allegiance to Satan. On a single night in March 1985, he killed Dayle Okazaki in Rosemead and then drove to Monterey Park, where he fatally shot Tsai-Lian Yu.

The Night Stalker's victims defied the typical serial killer profile. They ranged from nine-year-old Mei Leung, whose 1984 murder in a San Francisco hotel basement was linked to Ramirez through DNA in 2009, to elderly couples attacked in their beds. Vincent and Maxine Zazzara were killed on March 27, 1985, with Ramirez gouging out Maxine's eyes after her death. In August 1985, Ramirez traveled to San Francisco, where he murdered Peter and Barbara Pan. According to the IBTimes chronology and California court records, his total known victim count across both killing and non-fatal assaults ultimately encompassed over a dozen communities.

The investigation that led to Ramirez's identification involved multiple law enforcement agencies. According to the Malay Mail and LAPD case files, a pivotal break came on August 24, 1985, when thirteen-year-old James Romero III spotted a suspicious man in his Mission Viejo neighborhood and noted a partial license plate number of an orange Toyota. Police traced the car and found a fingerprint matching Ramirez, whose prints were already on file from earlier arrests. His photograph was released to the media on August 30, 1985.

The following day, August 31, 1985, Ramirez was recognized by residents of an East Los Angeles neighborhood as he attempted to steal a car. A group of citizens chased and beat him severely before police arrived to take him into custody. According to the Oxygen network's crime archive and multiple newspaper accounts, Ramirez was only narrowly saved from the mob by the arresting officers.

Ramirez's trial was one of the longest and most complex in California history, lasting from July 1988 until September 1989. According to UPI's trial coverage, the jury of seven women and five men found him guilty on all forty-three counts, including thirteen counts of murder. He was sentenced to death on November 7, 1989, receiving nineteen separate death sentences plus an additional fifty-nine years and four months in prison. Upon hearing the verdict, Ramirez reportedly told the courtroom that serial killing was not a big deal. He spent the remainder of his life on death row at San Quentin State Prison, where he attracted a cult following and married a female admirer in 1996. Richard Ramirez died of complications from B-cell lymphoma on June 7, 2013, at the age of fifty-three, having never faced execution.

name: Dennis Lynn Rader
victimProfile: Victims varied in age and gender; included families, single women, and elderly residents of the Wichita area, selected through stalking and surveillance
captureMethod: Rader sent a floppy disk to a Wichita TV station that contained recoverable metadata linking the file to his church computer and the name Dennis. DNA from a relative confirmed the match, leading to his arrest during a traffic stop.
sentence: 10 consecutive life sentences with a minimum term of 175 years without possibility of parole
fateDetail: Incarcerated at El Dorado Correctional Facility in Butler County, Kansas
summary: Dennis Rader, the BTK Killer, murdered 10 people in the Wichita, Kansas area between 1974 and 1991. He taunted police and media with letters for decades before a floppy disk led to his capture in 2005.
narrative: Dennis Lynn Rader was born on March 9, 1945, in Pittsburg, Kansas, the eldest of four sons born to William Elvin Rader and Dorothea Mae Cook. The family moved to Wichita when Rader was a young child. According to Biography.com and Kansas court records, Rader appeared to lead an unremarkable life on the surface. He served in the United States Air Force from 1966 to 1970, earned a degree in criminal justice from Wichita State University, and worked as an installer for ADT Security Services before becoming a compliance officer for Park City, Kansas.

Beneath this ordinary exterior, Rader harbored violent fantasies he would later describe in graphic detail to investigators. He admitted during his 2005 confession, documented by the Wichita Eagle, that he had fantasized about binding, torturing, and killing people since childhood. He created a self-styled acronym for his method: BTK, standing for Bind, Torture, Kill. His first attack, on January 15, 1974, targeted the Otero family in their Wichita home. Rader strangled Joseph Otero, 38, his wife Julie, 34, and two of their children, Josephine, 11, and Joseph Jr., 9, after cutting the phone lines and waiting inside for the family to return.

Rader killed sporadically over the next seventeen years, with long gaps between murders that made connecting the cases extraordinarily difficult for investigators. According to the Sedgwick County District Attorney's records and reporting by NBC News, his subsequent victims included Kathryn Bright, 21, who was stabbed on April 4, 1974; Shirley Vian, 24, strangled on March 17, 1977; and Nancy Fox, 25, strangled on December 8, 1977. After killing Fox, Rader called police to report the crime, and his voice was recorded on a dispatcher's tape. His later victims included Marine Hedge, 53, in April 1985; Vicki Wegerle, 28, in September 1986; and Dolores Davis, 62, in January 1991.

Throughout his criminal career, Rader sought public attention through a series of communications with police and media. According to the Wichita Eagle archive and FBI case files, he sent his first letter in 1974, shortly after the Otero murders, claiming responsibility and describing details only the killer would know. Over the following years, he sent poems, cryptic messages, and packages to news outlets, law enforcement, and even individual citizens. This pattern of communication, combined with the geographic concentration of killings in the Wichita area, became the defining feature of the BTK case.

After his final known murder in 1991, Rader went silent for over a decade, and the case went cold. Then, in March 2004, the Wichita Eagle published a retrospective article on the thirtieth anniversary of the Otero murders, and Rader resumed his communications. According to Oxygen's crime archive and CBS News reporting, he sent a series of packages to media outlets and police throughout 2004 and early 2005, containing identification cards from victims, word puzzles, and dolls arranged in bondage positions. In February 2005, he sent a floppy disk to KSAS-TV in Wichita, asking police whether the disk could be traced.

The disk proved to be Rader's undoing. Forensic analysts recovered metadata from a deleted Microsoft Word document on the disk. According to NBC News and the Wichita Police Department's case summary, the metadata contained the words 'Christ Lutheran Church' and listed the last user as 'Dennis.' Investigators quickly identified Rader as the president of the church's congregation council. They obtained a DNA sample from a medical record belonging to Rader's daughter and confirmed it was a familial match to evidence collected from crime scenes decades earlier.

Rader was arrested during a traffic stop near his Park City home on February 25, 2005. He subsequently confessed to all ten murders in extensive detail. Because Kansas had no death penalty at the time of the crimes, Rader could not be sentenced to death. On August 18, 2005, Judge Gregory Waller of the Sedgwick County District Court sentenced him to ten consecutive life sentences with a minimum term of 175 years without the possibility of parole. Rader remains incarcerated at the El Dorado Correctional Facility in Butler County, Kansas. His case is widely studied as an example of how digital forensic evidence can resolve long-dormant investigations.

name: Aileen Carol Wuornos
victimProfile: Middle-aged white men traveling alone on Florida highways, typically picked up as clients by Wuornos while she worked as a sex worker
captureMethod: After the abandoned car of victim Peter Siems was linked to two women matching Wuornos and her companion Tyria Moore, police located Wuornos at a Daytona Beach biker bar. Moore cooperated with investigators and helped elicit a confession.
sentence: Six death sentences for six counts of first-degree murder
fateDetail: Executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison in Starke, Florida on October 9, 2002
summary: Aileen Wuornos, one of America's most notorious female serial killers, shot and killed seven men along Florida highways in 1989-1990 while working as a sex worker. She was executed by lethal injection in 2002.
narrative: Aileen Carol Pittman was born on February 29, 1956, in Rochester, Michigan, a suburb of Detroit. Her father, Leo Dale Pittman, was a convicted child molester who was later diagnosed with schizophrenia and hanged himself in prison. Her mother, Diane Wuornos, abandoned Aileen and her older brother Keith when they were toddlers, and the children were adopted by their maternal grandparents, Lauri and Britta Wuornos. According to Britannica and court records from the State of Florida, Wuornos endured severe abuse from her grandfather and became pregnant at age fourteen, allegedly after being raped by a family friend.

After giving birth to a son who was placed for adoption, Wuornos was thrown out of the family home and began living in the woods and supporting herself through petty crime and sex work. According to Biography.com and investigative reporting by AETV, she spent the next two decades drifting across the country, accumulating arrests for armed robbery, assault, forgery, and other offenses. In 1986, she began a relationship with hotel maid Tyria Moore in Daytona Beach, Florida, and the two women lived together in motels while Wuornos continued to solicit men along the Interstate 75 corridor.

Wuornos's killing spree began on November 30, 1989, when fifty-one-year-old Richard Mallory, the owner of a Clearwater electronics repair shop, disappeared after leaving his business. His fully clothed body was found on December 13, 1989, in a wooded area near Ormond Beach, shot multiple times with a .22 caliber handgun. According to the Volusia County Sheriff's Office records and reporting by Forbes, Wuornos would later claim that Mallory had raped her and that the killing was self-defense. Subsequent investigation revealed that Mallory had previously served time for sexual assault, adding complexity to the legal arguments.

Over the following twelve months, Wuornos killed six more men along Florida highways. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement case files and reporting by AllThatsInteresting.com, her victims included David Spears, a construction worker found on June 1, 1990; Charles Carskaddon, a rodeo worker found on June 6; Peter Siems, a retired merchant seaman whose body was never recovered; Troy Burress, a sausage salesman found on August 4; Charles Humphreys, a former police chief and child abuse investigator found on September 12; and Walter Antonio, a trucker and reserve police officer found on November 19. Each victim had been shot with a .22 caliber pistol.

The investigation gained traction in July 1990, when Wuornos and Moore were involved in a car accident while driving Peter Siems's vehicle. Witnesses provided descriptions of two women, and police were able to connect the abandoned car to the missing man. According to the Clark County Prosecutor's archive and Investigation Discovery's case file, investigators traced the descriptions to aliases used by Wuornos and eventually identified her through pawnshop records and fingerprints. She was arrested on January 9, 1991, at the Last Resort bar in Harbor Oaks, near Daytona Beach.

After Wuornos's arrest, detectives persuaded Tyria Moore to cooperate with the investigation. Moore made recorded telephone calls from a hotel room to Wuornos in jail, during which Wuornos confessed in order to protect Moore from prosecution. According to the Volusia County court transcript and Florida Supreme Court records, Wuornos initially maintained that all seven killings were acts of self-defense against men who had raped or attempted to rape her during encounters along the highway. This defense was largely rejected by juries and judges across multiple trials.

Wuornos was tried first for the murder of Richard Mallory in January 1992 and convicted of first-degree murder. She received the death penalty. She was subsequently convicted and sentenced to death in five additional cases, though she was never tried for the murder of Peter Siems because his body was never found. In the years before her execution, Wuornos became increasingly erratic, at times recanting her self-defense claims and at other times insisting she had been treated unfairly. Governor Jeb Bush ordered a psychiatric evaluation, and the examining psychiatrists concluded she was mentally competent. Aileen Wuornos was executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison on October 9, 2002, at the age of forty-six. Her life was later dramatized in the 2003 film Monster, for which Charlize Theron won the Academy Award for Best Actress.

name: David Richard Berkowitz
victimProfile: Young men and women, predominantly couples sitting in parked cars in the boroughs of the Bronx, Queens, and Brooklyn
captureMethod: A parking ticket placed on Berkowitz's car near the scene of his final shooting led police to his Yonkers apartment, where they found his .44 caliber Bulldog revolver in the vehicle.
sentence: Six consecutive 25-years-to-life sentences, totaling 365 years in prison
fateDetail: Incarcerated at Shawangunk Correctional Facility, a maximum-security prison in Wallkill, New York. Has been denied parole multiple times since becoming eligible in 2002.
summary: David Berkowitz, the Son of Sam, terrorized New York City in 1976-77, shooting young couples with a .44 caliber revolver. He killed six and wounded seven, taunting police with letters before a parking ticket led to his arrest.
narrative: David Richard Berkowitz was born Richard David Falco on June 1, 1953, in Brooklyn, New York. He was the illegitimate son of Betty Broder, a married woman who had an affair with real estate agent Joseph Klineman. Unable to raise the child, Broder gave him up for adoption to Nathan and Pearl Berkowitz, a middle-class Jewish couple from the Bronx who renamed him David. According to Britannica and EBSCO's biographical research archive, Berkowitz was a troubled child who set fires and bullied other children, though he was of above-average intelligence. His adoptive mother died of breast cancer in 1967, an event that profoundly affected the fourteen-year-old.

Berkowitz served in the United States Army from 1971 to 1974, including a posting in South Korea. After his discharge, he returned to New York and worked as a letter sorter for the United States Postal Service. According to AETV's case file and the Vintti legal archive, he began experiencing increasingly violent fantasies and claimed to hear demonic voices commanding him to kill. He would later tell police that the commands came through a demon-possessed Labrador retriever belonging to his Yonkers neighbor, Sam Carr, a claim from which his infamous moniker would derive.

Berkowitz's first documented attacks occurred in December 1975, when he stabbed two women in separate incidents in the Bronx's Co-op City neighborhood. Both survived, and the attacks were not connected to him until after his arrest. His shooting spree began on July 29, 1976, when he approached a car parked outside an apartment building in the Pelham Bay section of the Bronx and opened fire with a Charter Arms .44 Bulldog revolver. Eighteen-year-old Donna Lauria was killed instantly, and her friend Jody Valenti was wounded. According to History.com's crime archive and the New York City Police Department case files, this was the first of eight separate shooting attacks over the next thirteen months.

Throughout the fall of 1976 and into 1977, Berkowitz continued to target young people in parked cars across the Bronx, Queens, and Brooklyn. His victims included Carl Denaro, shot in October 1976, and Donna DeMasi and Joanne Lomino, wounded in November 1976. In January 1977, he killed Christine Freund, and in March, he shot and killed Virginia Voskerichian. On April 17, 1977, he murdered both Valentina Suriani and Alexander Esau, leaving a handwritten letter at the scene addressed to NYPD Captain Joseph Borrelli, signed 'Son of Sam.' According to the Crime and Investigation network's timeline and reporting by Biography.com, this letter launched one of the most intense media frenzies in New York history.

Berkowitz wrote a second letter, this time to New York Daily News columnist Jimmy Breslin, taunting police and the public. The letter, postmarked May 30, 1977, was front-page news and plunged the city into a state of fear. Women in the affected neighborhoods reportedly dyed their hair blonde or cut it short because several victims had long brown hair. According to the New York City Police Department's Operation Omega task force records, more than three hundred detectives were assigned to the case at its peak, making it the largest manhunt in New York City history.

Berkowitz's final attack occurred on July 31, 1977, in the Bath Beach section of Brooklyn, where he shot Robert Violante and Stacy Moskowitz as they sat in a parked car. Moskowitz, age twenty, died from her wounds, and Violante lost his left eye and most of the vision in his right. A witness named Cacilia Davis noticed a man removing a parking ticket from a car near the scene shortly before the shooting. According to History.com and the subsequent investigation records, detectives traced the ticket to a cream-colored Ford Galaxie registered to David Berkowitz at 35 Pine Street in Yonkers.

On August 10, 1977, police staked out Berkowitz's apartment and found the .44 Bulldog revolver in a paper bag on the passenger seat of his car, along with a threatening letter and a submachine gun. When Berkowitz emerged from his building, he was arrested without resistance. According to the Vintti legal archive and New York State court records, he confessed immediately, telling officers with a smile that they had found him. He pleaded guilty to six counts of second-degree murder in May 1978, rejecting his attorneys' advice to pursue an insanity defense. In June 1978, Judge Joseph Corso sentenced him to six consecutive sentences of twenty-five years to life, totaling 365 years. Berkowitz remains incarcerated at the Shawangunk Correctional Facility in Wallkill, New York, and has been denied parole at every hearing since becoming eligible in 2002. His case inspired New York's 'Son of Sam' law, which initially sought to prevent criminals from profiting through media deals, though the statute was later struck down by the United States Supreme Court in 1991.
